content: Efforts to reduce tobacco use should include structural and environmental interventions such as increasing excise taxes on tobacco products to make them less affordable. Comprehensive bans on tobacco advertising, promotion, and sponsorship—including cross-border advertising and online platforms—should be enforced. Additionally, promoting smoke-free entertainment media, cinema, and drama is essential. Smoke-free environments should be established through laws that prohibit smoking in schools, recreational areas, indoor workplaces, public spaces, and public transport. Organizational and community-level interventions should focus on raising awareness about the dangers of tobacco through regular, effective mass media campaigns. Packaging and advertising should include pictorial health warnings. Tobacco prevention should be integrated into school policies, skill-based health education, and health services. These programs must not involve collaboration with or funding from the tobacco industry. At the interpersonal and individual level, clinicians should encourage non-smokers to avoid starting smoking, strongly advise smokers to quit, and support their cessation efforts. Individuals using other forms of tobacco should also be advised to stop. The WHO’s toolkit for delivering brief tobacco interventions in primary care provides specific guidance. Physical activity is critical for preventing and managing non-communicable diseases (NCDs) such as heart disease, stroke, diabetes, and certain cancers. It also helps prevent hypertension, maintain a healthy weight, and improve mental health and overall well-being. However, over 80% of adolescents worldwide are insufficiently active. Governments should collaborate with communities, private sectors, and NGOs to create safe spaces for physical activity and accessible sports facilities. Schools and public spaces should provide adequate facilities for physical activity, including gender-friendly spaces where appropriate. Public awareness programs should educate children, adolescents, parents, caregivers, teachers, and health professionals about healthy body size, physical activity, sleep behaviors, and appropriate screen time use. Schools should implement physical education curricula that promote lifelong physical activity and provide inclusive opportunities for all children, including those with specific needs. Regular, structured sports activities should be encouraged to reduce sedentary behaviors and strengthen the link between physical activity and health. Adolescents should engage in at least 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous physical activity daily, including aerobic and muscle-strengthening activities at least three times a week. Sedentary time, particularly recreational screen time, should be limited. Community-based initiatives should provide free, enjoyable, and culturally appropriate physical activities. Optimal nutrition during adolescence is crucial for current and future health. Nutritional deficiencies from childhood can be addressed during this period, and catch-up growth may be possible. Challenges such as micronutrient deficiencies, food insecurity, poor diet quality, and obesity must be tackled through coordinated actions involving health, education, social protection, and media sectors. Schools can target high-risk groups with interventions like iron and folic acid supplementation for adolescent girls. Health professionals should implement screening and treatment programs and provide trusted nutritional information. Structural interventions to promote healthy diets include developing nutrient profiles to identify unhealthy foods, implementing standardized global nutrient labeling systems, and taxing energy-dense, nutrient-poor foods and sugar-sweetened beverages. Governments should restrict the availability of highly processed foods and reduce the marketing impact of unhealthy products. Schools and public institutions should create healthy food environments and improve access to affordable, nutritious foods, particularly in disadvantaged communities. Nutrition education should cover dietary diversity, food preparation skills, and growing school gardens. Micronutrient fortification and supplementation are essential for adolescents. Staple foods like flour should be fortified with iron and folic acid to prevent deficiencies and reduce the risk of neural tube defects. Salt should be fortified with iodine to prevent iodine deficiency disorders. Daily iron supplementation is recommended for menstruating women and adolescent girls in areas with high anemia prevalence. Intermittent iron and folic acid supplementation can also improve hemoglobin levels and reduce anemia risk. In humanitarian and fragile settings, adolescents face increased risks and vulnerabilities. Interventions should include ageand gender-responsive programs that protect and support young people. Core health services, including rehabilitation and essential medicines, must be accessible to adolescents with disabilities or injuries. Survivors of violence should receive medical care, psychosocial support, and reintegration assistance. Safe spaces, both virtual and physical, should be created, including in schools. Sexual and reproductive health (SRH) interventions should include contraceptive and condom use education, STI and HIV prevention, and psychosocial support. Minimal SRH service packages should be implemented, with a focus on addressing sexual violence, child marriage, and family planning. Mental health interventions should promote inclusive recreational activities, education, and purposeful engagement. Psychological first aid techniques should support adolescents and their families. Non-specialist healthcare providers should follow WHO guidelines for managing adolescent mental, neurological, and substance-use conditions. Play-based programs using sports and recreation can be effective, particularly in refugee centers and adolescent-friendly spaces. National governments must prioritize adolescent health and well-being programs, considering the unique needs and resource constraints of each country.
